sections.title: How does the Torsional spring calculator work?
sections.html:
The Torsional spring calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports wire diameter (d) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the spring index (C), number of active turns (Na), the young modulus (E) and the length, first end (l1).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Torsional spring calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Wire diameter (d)=spring diameter (D) ÷ spring index (C)
Ends contribution (Ne)=number of active turns (Na) − numbers of full turns (Nb)
Spring diameter (D)=(1 ÷ 3) × (length, first end (l1) + length, second end (l2)) ÷ (PI × ends contribution (Ne))
Wire diameter (d)=length (L) ÷ (numbers of full turns (Nb) + 1)
Arm (r)=torque (M) ÷ applied force (F)
Stress correction factor, inner (Ki)=(1 ÷ 4) × (4 × (spring index (C) ^ 2) − spring index (C) − 1) ÷ (spring index (C) × (spring index (C) − 1))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Spring diameter (D) = 30 mm and Spring index (C) = 10. The calculator returns Wire diameter (d) = 3 mm, Stress correction factor, inner (Ki) = 1.0806 and Stress correction factor, outer (Ko) = 0.9295.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Wire diameter (d) = 3 mm, Stress correction factor, inner (Ki) = 1.0806 and Stress correction factor, outer (Ko) = 0.9295 should be roughly the size you expected from Spring diameter (D) = 30 mm and Spring index (C) = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Torsional spring calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the spring index, number of active turns and the young modulus — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Torsional spring calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns wire diameter (d), derived from the spring index, number of active turns and the young modulus. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Torsional spring calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the spring index, number of active turns, the young modulus and the length, first end, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter spring diameter (D) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Spring diameter (D) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Wire diameter (d) = 3 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Torsional spring calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
